subjects.name: Naturwissenschaften
subjects.description: In Kl. 5/6 the sciences are taught either as an integrated subject (BW 'Biologie, Naturphänomene und Technik', Bayern 'Natur und Technik', Berlin/Brandenburg 'Naturwissenschaften 5/6') or as separate Biologie and Physik (NRW Gymnasium, Erprobungsstufe); Chemie usually starts in Kl. 7, but substance properties and separation appear in the integrated subjects.

subjects.name: Erdkunde
subjects.description: Called Erdkunde (NRW, Hessen), Geographie (BW, Bayern) or Geografie (Berlin/Brandenburg, inside 'Gesellschaftswissenschaften 5/6'); Kl. 5/6 focuses on map skills, Planet Earth, Germany's landscapes and how people live and work in rural, urban and tourist regions of Germany and Europe.

subjects.name: Geschichte
subjects.description: Usually starts in Kl. 6 (NRW G9, BW and Bayern Gymnasium), sometimes Kl. 5 or only Kl. 7; Kl. 5/6 covers historical method, prehistory, Egypt, Greece, Rome (incl. Romans and Germanic peoples) and, in several Länder, the Frankish kingdom.

subjects.name: Politik und Wirtschaft
subjects.description: Civic and economic education under many names (NRW 'Wirtschaft-Politik', Berlin/Brandenburg 'Politische Bildung' inside Gesellschaftswissenschaften 5/6, 'Gesellschaftslehre' at comprehensive schools); in Bayern and BW Gymnasium it only starts in Kl. 7 or later. Kl. 5/6 starts from pupils' own life: family, school democracy, the municipality, children's rights, pocket money, advertising and media.

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: The Scientific Method Cycle
topics.description: Pupils learn the German 'Erkenntnisweg' as a fixed sequence: observe a phenomenon, ask a question, state a testable Vermutung (hypothesis), plan and run an experiment, and check whether the result supports the hypothesis. Observation (Beobachtung) and interpretation (Deutung) are written separately.
evidence: Formulates a testable hypothesis ('Ich vermute, dass …, weil …') for an observed phenomenon such as a sinking candle
Keeps observation and explanation apart when describing an experiment
States whether a result confirms or refutes the hypothesis and suggests what to test next
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} noticed that ice cubes melt faster in salt water than in tap water, could they turn this into a question, a hypothesis and a simple experiment that tests it?

externalPrerequisites.subject: Sachunterricht
externalPrerequisites.concept: carrying out simple guided experiments and making predictions (Vermutungen) in primary science
externalPrerequisites.reason: Kl. 5 formalises the inquiry steps pupils met informally in Sachunterricht

osMatches.note: os covers only comparing results with predictions (age 4-8)
os covers only the conclusion step

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Writing a Lab Report
topics.description: Pupils write a standard German Versuchsprotokoll with the headings Fragestellung, Vermutung, Material, Durchführung (incl. labelled sketch of the set-up), Beobachtung and Auswertung/Deutung. The protocol is a recurring assessed format from Kl. 5 onwards.
evidence: Writes a complete protocol with all standard headings for an experiment they carried out
Draws a labelled cross-section sketch of the apparatus
Writes observations in the past tense without interpretation and puts the explanation under Auswertung
topics.assessmentPrompt: After filtering muddy water in class, could {{name}} write a protocol with question, hypothesis, materials, procedure sketch, observation and explanation in the right sections?

prerequisites.reason: The protocol headings mirror the steps of the Erkenntnisweg

externalPrerequisites.subject: Deutsch
externalPrerequisites.concept: writing short structured factual texts (Sachtexte) with headings
externalPrerequisites.reason: Protocol writing relies on basic expository writing

osMatches.note: os focuses on recording data, not the full protocol format
os places full science reports at age 13-14; German pupils start at age 10-11

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Measuring and Graphing Results
topics.description: Pupils measure physical quantities as Maßzahl plus Einheit with suitable instruments, record repeated readings in tables, and present them as bar or line graphs (e.g. a temperature-time curve). They recognise reading errors and why measurements beat subjective senses.
evidence: Records measurements with number and unit in a prepared table
Draws a line graph with labelled axes and a sensible scale from a measurement series
Names one source of measurement or reading error and how to reduce it
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measured the temperature of cooling tea every two minutes, could they put the values in a table and draw a correctly labelled line graph?

prerequisites.reason: Measuring is embedded in planned experiments

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: measuring quantities with units (Größen: Länge, Masse, Zeit) and converting units
externalPrerequisites.reason: Science measurement builds directly on Größen und Messen

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: reading and drawing bar charts and tables (Daten)
externalPrerequisites.reason: Graphing results extends data representation from mathematics

osMatches.note: os places tables, charts and graphs at age 12-13

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Controlling Variables
topics.description: Pupils plan experiments in which only one factor is changed while all others are kept constant, and they use a control set-up (Kontrollansatz). The classic Kl. 5/6 context is germination: water, warmth, light and air are varied one at a time.
evidence: Names the changed, measured and constant factors in a planned experiment
Designs a control set-up for comparison
Explains why a test that changes two factors at once gives no clear answer
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wanted to find out whether cress seeds need light to germinate, could they set up dishes that change only the light and keep water, warmth and seed number the same?

prerequisites.reason: Variable control refines the experiment step of the cycle
Comparing set-ups requires measured outcomes

osMatches.note: os 'fair testing' at age 7-10 is the same idea at a lower level

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Lab Safety Rules
topics.description: Pupils learn the rules of the science room (Fachraum): safety goggles, tied-back hair, no eating, emergency stop switch, fire blanket and eye shower, and the meaning of GHS hazard pictograms. The rules follow the KMK safety guideline for teaching (RiSU) and are often signed by pupils.
evidence: Explains the purpose of at least five lab rules and points out the emergency switch, eye shower and fire blanket
Matches common GHS pictograms (flammable, corrosive, harmful) to their meaning
Behaves according to the rules during a practical without reminders
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw a bottle with a red-bordered flame pictogram in the science room, could they say what it means and which precautions to take?

externalPrerequisites.subject: Sachunterricht
externalPrerequisites.concept: following safety rules when experimenting with heat, water and tools in primary school
externalPrerequisites.reason: Builds on basic safe-experimenting habits

osMatches.note: os is generic safe procedures; no fixed lab rules or GHS pictograms
os covers general health and safety signs (age 5-7)

topics.laenderNotes: Safety instruction (Sicherheitsbelehrung) at the start of each school year is required by the KMK 'Richtlinie zur Sicherheit im Unterricht' (RiSU) in all Länder.

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Using a Gas Burner
topics.description: Pupils light, regulate and switch off a Teclu or Bunsen burner in the correct order, distinguish the luminous yellow flame from the hot non-luminous blue flame, and heat a test tube safely (angled, never pointing at people). It is the first 'Führerschein' style skill in German science lessons.
evidence: Lights and extinguishes the burner in the correct sequence (gas tap, lighter, air supply)
Explains the difference between the luminous and the non-luminous flame and where the flame is hottest
Heats a liquid in a test tube safely using a holder and correct angle
topics.assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} light a gas burner on their own, turn it into a hot blue flame and safely warm water in a test tube?

prerequisites.reason: Burner use is only permitted after the safety instruction

topics.laenderNotes: The Teclu burner is standard in German, Austrian and Swiss schools; many schools issue a 'Brennerführerschein' in Kl. 5/6.

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Characteristics of Living Things
topics.description: Pupils use a fixed list of criteria (Bewegung, Reizbarkeit, Stoffwechsel, Wachstum, Entwicklung, Fortpflanzung, Aufbau aus Zellen) to decide whether something is alive. Only things showing all criteria count as living; borderline cases like a candle flame or a car are discussed.
evidence: Lists the characteristics of living things
Applies all criteria to decide whether a plant, a flame and a robot are alive
Explains why one criterion alone (e.g. movement) is not enough
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked whether a candle flame is alive because it 'grows' and 'needs air', could they use the full list of criteria to explain why it is not?

externalPrerequisites.subject: Sachunterricht
externalPrerequisites.concept: distinguishing living and non-living things and what plants and animals need
externalPrerequisites.reason: Kl. 5 systematises an idea introduced in primary school

osMatches.note: os 'Living, Dead & Never Alive' (age 6-9) without the formal criteria list

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Using a Light Microscope
topics.description: Pupils name the parts of a light microscope, prepare a wet mount (Frischpräparat) such as onion epidermis, focus from low to high magnification, calculate total magnification and make a scientific drawing (Zeichnung nach Vorgaben).
evidence: Names the main parts (ocular, objective, stage, coarse and fine focus, light source) and their function
Prepares an onion-skin wet mount and focuses it starting with the lowest magnification
Calculates total magnification and produces a labelled pencil drawing
topics.assessmentPrompt: Given an onion and a microscope, could {{name}} prepare a slide, find the cells and draw what they see with labels and the magnification?

prerequisites.reason: Handling glass slides and equipment follows lab rules

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: multiplying whole numbers (magnification = ocular × objective)
externalPrerequisites.reason: Needed to compute total magnification

osMatches.note: os places this at age 11-12; German pupils start at age 10-11

topics.laenderNotes: NRW and Berlin/Brandenburg place light microscopy in Kl. 5/6; BW BNT 5/6 only requires magnifier/stereo magnifier, so microscopy often starts with Biologie in Kl. 7.

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Plant and Animal Cells
topics.description: Pupils learn that all living things are built of cells, name the light-microscope structures (Zellmembran, Zellplasma, Zellkern; in plants also Zellwand, Vakuole, Chloroplasten) and order the system levels Zelle – Gewebe – Organ – Organismus.
evidence: Labels the visible structures of plant and animal cells
States two differences between plant and animal cells and links chloroplasts to plants' way of feeding
Orders cell, tissue, organ and organism with one example each
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked at a drawing of an unknown cell with a cell wall and green chloroplasts, could they say whether it came from a plant or an animal and why?

prerequisites.reason: Cells are discovered and compared through microscope work
Being built of cells is one of the characteristics of life

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Dog and Cat as Mammals
topics.nameDe: Hund und Katze – Säugetiere als Haustiere
topics.description: Using the dog (Hetzjäger, descended from the wolf) and the cat (Schleichjäger, Zehengänger with retractable claws) pupils learn the typical mammal features (fur, lungs, constant body temperature, live birth, suckling) and how body build fits hunting style. Domestication and breeding explain why dogs differ from wolves.
evidence: Lists five features that make dog and cat mammals
Compares how dog and cat hunt and relates this to their senses, legs and claws
Explains that dog breeds arose from wolves through breeding by humans
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watched a cat stalk a bird and a dog chase a ball, could they explain how each animal's body and senses fit its way of hunting?

prerequisites.reason: Animal study starts from the characteristics of living things

externalPrerequisites.subject: Sachunterricht
externalPrerequisites.concept: pets and their needs; naming common animal groups
externalPrerequisites.reason: Pupils bring everyday knowledge of pets from primary school

osMatches.note: os distinguishes wild, farm and pet animals (age 5-8) without anatomy

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Teeth Types and Diet
topics.description: Pupils compare the Raubtiergebiss (dog: Fangzähne, Reißzähne), the Pflanzenfressergebiss (cattle: no upper incisors, broad grinding molars) and the Allesfressergebiss (pig, human), and explain the cow as a Wiederkäuer with a four-chambered stomach.
evidence: Identifies a carnivore, herbivore and omnivore skull from its teeth
Explains the function of canines, carnassials and grinding molars
Describes the path of food through the ruminant stomach in the right order
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were shown the skull of a dog and of a cow, could they say which is which and explain how the teeth fit the food?

prerequisites.reason: The carnivore dentition is introduced with the dog

osMatches.note: os herbivore/carnivore/omnivore at age 5-6 without dentition detail

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Livestock Farming and Animal Welfare
topics.description: Pupils compare forms of keeping farm animals (e.g. laying hens in Boden-, Freiland- and Biohaltung, read via the EU egg code 0–3; pigs, cattle), relate them to the animals' natural needs, and form a reasoned judgement about artgerechte Haltung and consumer choices.
evidence: Decodes the first digit of an egg stamp and describes the matching husbandry form
Compares two husbandry forms against the animal's natural behaviour
Gives a reasoned personal judgement weighing animal welfare, price and environment
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} found the code '0-DE-…' and '3-DE-…' on two egg boxes, could they explain what the numbers mean for the hens and argue which eggs they would buy?

prerequisites.reason: Knowledge of cattle and pigs as farm animals
Concept of domestication and keeping needs

osMatches.note: os describes raising farm animals (age 6-8) without evaluating welfare

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Birds Adapted for Flight
topics.description: Pupils explain how birds are built for flight: lightweight hollow bones, feathers (Konturfeder, Daunenfeder), strong breast muscles and a streamlined body; they distinguish gliding and flapping flight and compare Nesthocker and Nestflüchter.
evidence: Explains three features of the bird body that save weight or provide lift
Compares a bird bone with a mammal bone and interprets the difference
Distinguishes altricial and precocial chicks with one example each
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} held a cut chicken bone and a beef bone, could they explain what the difference tells us about how birds can fly?

prerequisites.reason: Bird anatomy is compared with the mammal body plan

osMatches.note: os structural adaptations in general (age 9-11); no flight-specific topic

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Fish Adapted to Water
topics.nameDe: Fische: Angepasstheit an das Leben im Wasser
topics.description: Pupils describe fish features (streamlined body, scales and mucus, fins, gills, swim bladder, lateral line, external fertilisation via Laich) as adaptations to life in water, explaining breathing and hovering (Schweben) in water.
evidence: Explains how gills take oxygen from water
Explains the function of the swim bladder for hovering at a depth
Relates body shape and fins to energy-efficient swimming
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watched a goldfish hovering still in the middle of a tank, could they explain how it stays at that depth and how it breathes?

prerequisites.reason: Breathing and movement are criteria of life applied to water animals

osMatches.note: os classifies ocean animals; gills/scales mentioned, no swim bladder

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Amphibians and Their Protection
topics.description: Using frog and toad, pupils describe the metamorphosis from spawn to tadpole (gills) to frog (lungs and skin breathing), explain why amphibians depend on water and moist habitats, and discuss threats and protection such as toad-crossing fences (Krötenzäune) during spring migration.
evidence: Orders and describes the stages of frog development, including the change in breathing
Explains why amphibians need both water and land habitats
Names two threats to native amphibians and a protection measure
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw volunteers setting up a low fence along a road in March, could they explain what it is for and why toads are at risk?

prerequisites.reason: Gill breathing of tadpoles is understood by comparison with fish

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Reptiles Adapted to Land
topics.description: Using native examples (Zauneidechse, Ringelnatter) pupils explain how reptiles are independent of water: dry horny scales, lung breathing, internal fertilisation and shelled eggs. As cold-blooded animals they warm up in the sun.
evidence: Names three reptile features that allow life away from water
Compares reptile and amphibian skin, breathing and eggs
Explains why a lizard basks in the sun in the morning
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} found a lizard sunning itself on a warm wall, could they explain why it does this and why, unlike a frog, it can live in a dry place?

prerequisites.reason: Reptile features are explained in contrast to amphibians

osMatches.note: os compares external features of animal groups at age 5-7

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Comparing the Vertebrate Classes
topics.description: Pupils compare fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals by skin covering, breathing, body temperature (wechselwarm/gleichwarm) and reproduction, assign unknown species to a class by criteria and see the order as a hint of evolutionary relationship.
evidence: Completes a comparison table of the five classes for skin, breathing, body temperature and reproduction
Assigns borderline animals (whale, bat, penguin, salamander) to the correct class with reasons
Distinguishes cold-blooded and warm-blooded animals
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were told that whales live in the sea and look like fish, could they use the class criteria to prove that whales are mammals?

prerequisites.reason: Mammal features are the reference class
Bird features are needed for the comparison
Fish features are needed for the comparison
Reptile and amphibian features complete the comparison

osMatches.note: os at age 5-7, external features only

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: How Animals Survive Winter
topics.description: Pupils distinguish the German triad Winterschlaf (hedgehog, dormouse: body temperature drops sharply), Winterruhe (squirrel, badger: wakes to feed) and Winterstarre/Kältestarre (frog, lizard: cold-blooded, body temperature follows surroundings), plus winter fur, fat reserves and bird migration.
evidence: Assigns hedgehog, squirrel and frog to the correct overwintering strategy
Explains each strategy in terms of body temperature and energy use
Explains why only warm-blooded animals can hibernate in the strict sense
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} found a hedgehog asleep under leaves in January and a squirrel digging up nuts, could they explain the difference between how the two animals survive winter?

prerequisites.reason: Requires the distinction between warm- and cold-blooded animals

osMatches.note: os mentions hibernation only as a behavioural adaptation example

topics.laenderNotes: The three-way Winterschlaf/Winterruhe/Winterstarre distinction is a standard German textbook topic (BW BNT 3.1.4(12); BB Naturwissenschaften 5/6 Themenfeld 3.3 'Die Sonne als Energiequelle').

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Insects: Body Plan and Metamorphosis
topics.description: Using bee or May beetle, pupils describe the insect body plan (head, thorax, abdomen; six legs; exoskeleton; tracheae), compare it with vertebrates, and distinguish complete (egg–larva–pupa–adult) and incomplete metamorphosis.
evidence: Labels the three body sections and states two differences to a vertebrate
Orders the stages of complete metamorphosis for a butterfly or beetle
Distinguishes complete and incomplete metamorphosis with an example each
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} found a caterpillar and a grasshopper nymph, could they explain how each develops into an adult and which one has a pupa stage?

prerequisites.reason: Invertebrates are introduced by contrast with vertebrates

topics.laenderNotes: Invertebrates are a BW BNT section (3.1.7); NRW Biologie 5/6 focuses on vertebrates and seed plants.

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Organs of a Flowering Plant
topics.description: Pupils name root, shoot axis (Sprossachse), leaf and flower and explain how they work together: roots anchor and take up water and minerals, the stem transports, leaves produce food, and flowers serve reproduction.
evidence: Labels the organs on a whole plant
Explains the function of each organ
Describes the path of water from the soil to the leaves
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} put a white flower in coloured water, could they predict what happens and explain which plant organs are involved?

prerequisites.reason: Plants are studied as living organisms

externalPrerequisites.subject: Sachunterricht
externalPrerequisites.concept: parts of a plant and what plants need to grow
externalPrerequisites.reason: Kl. 5 adds functions and the system view

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Flower Structure
topics.description: Pupils dissect a flower (e.g. cherry or rapeseed) from outside in and lay out a Legebild of sepals, petals, stamens (anther, filament) and pistil (stigma, style, ovary), naming the male and female parts.
evidence: Dissects a flower and arranges a correctly labelled Legebild
Identifies stamens as male and pistil as female parts
Counts and records the number of each flower part
topics.assessmentPrompt: Given a fresh tulip or cherry blossom, could {{name}} take it apart, lay out the parts in order and name the male and female parts?

prerequisites.reason: The flower is studied as one of the plant organs

osMatches.note: os flower structure is bundled with reproduction at age 12-13

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Pollination and Fertilisation
topics.description: Pupils distinguish pollination (transfer of pollen by insects or wind) from fertilisation (fusion of pollen and egg cell after the pollen tube grows), describe how the ovary becomes a fruit and the ovule a seed, and contrast this with vegetative propagation (runners, tubers).
evidence: Explains the difference between pollination and fertilisation
Describes how a cherry fruit develops from the flower
Gives one example each of insect pollination, wind pollination and vegetative propagation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard that a cherry tree gives no fruit after a cold, bee-less spring, could they explain the chain from pollination to fruit?

prerequisites.reason: Requires knowing stamens, stigma and ovary

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Seed and Fruit Dispersal
topics.description: Pupils classify dispersal by wind (dandelion, maple 'Propeller'), animals (burrs, berries eaten), water and self-dispersal, relate fruit structure to dispersal, and test this with simple functional models such as paper helicopters.
evidence: Assigns given fruits to a dispersal type based on their structure
Builds and tests a model of a wind-dispersed fruit, changing one variable
Explains why dispersal is an advantage for the plant
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} found a maple seed spinning to the ground, could they explain how its shape helps the tree and design a paper model to test it?

prerequisites.reason: Fruits and seeds result from fertilisation
Model experiments vary one factor

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Seed Structure and Germination
topics.description: Pupils describe the structure of a bean seed (seed coat, cotyledons with stored food, embryo) and find out by controlled experiments that germination needs water, warmth and air but not light, distinguishing germination from later growth.
evidence: Labels seed coat, cotyledons and embryo on a soaked bean
Plans a germination experiment with a control set-up for one condition
States the germination conditions and explains why light is not needed at first
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} set up cress seeds on dry cotton, wet cotton, in the fridge and in a dark cupboard, could they predict and explain which ones would germinate?

prerequisites.reason: Germination conditions are found by varying one factor at a time
The seedling develops root and shoot

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Introduction to Photosynthesis
topics.description: Pupils state photosynthesis as a word equation (water + carbon dioxide → glucose + oxygen, using light energy in chloroplasts) and explain why it is the basis of food and oxygen for animals and humans.
evidence: Writes the word equation of photosynthesis with light energy and chlorophyll
Explains where the plant's substances come from (air and water, not soil)
Explains why animals depend on plants for food and oxygen
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked where the wood of a huge oak tree comes from, could they explain that it is built mostly from air and water using sunlight?

prerequisites.reason: Leaves as organs of food production
Chloroplasts are the site of photosynthesis

osMatches.note: os 'Plants grow from air and water' (age 10-11)

topics.laenderNotes: NRW requires the word equation in Kl. 5/6; BW BNT 5/6 only covers the energy chain Sun → plant → human, formal photosynthesis follows in Biologie from Kl. 7.

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Identifying Plants with a Key
topics.description: Pupils use a dichotomous identification key (printed or app) to identify native flowering plants and trees, recognise families such as Kreuzblütler, Lippenblütler or Rosengewächse by flower structure, and press and label specimens in a herbarium.
evidence: Identifies an unknown native plant by working step by step through a dichotomous key
Assigns plants to a family using flower features
Names and recognises two or three native deciduous and coniferous trees
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} collected a flowering plant on a school walk, could they identify it with a key and say which family it belongs to?

prerequisites.reason: Keys and families rely on flower structure

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Skeleton, Joints and Muscles
topics.description: Pupils name the main sections of the skeleton and their functions (support, protection, movement), distinguish joint types (ball-and-socket, hinge), explain the double-S-shaped spine and the antagonist principle (Gegenspielerprinzip) of biceps and triceps, and discuss posture damage from heavy school bags.
evidence: Labels skull, spine, rib cage, shoulder and pelvic girdle and limbs
Explains with a model how biceps and triceps move the forearm
Matches joint types to examples and their range of movement
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} bent and stretched their arm while holding the other hand on the upper arm, could they explain which muscle works when and why muscles always work in pairs?

externalPrerequisites.subject: Sachunterricht
externalPrerequisites.concept: naming body parts and basic knowledge of bones and muscles
externalPrerequisites.reason: Builds on primary body knowledge

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Nutrients and a Balanced Diet
topics.description: Pupils name carbohydrates, fats and proteins plus vitamins, minerals, fibre and water and their roles, test foods with simple Nährstoffnachweise (iodine for starch, grease-spot test for fat), and assess a day's meals against the DGE nutrition circle or food pyramid and energy needs.
evidence: Carries out and documents the iodine starch test and the fat spot test
Names the main function of each nutrient group
Evaluates a given daily menu and suggests improvements for a balanced diet
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wrote down everything they ate in a day, could they check it against the food pyramid and suggest one concrete improvement?

prerequisites.reason: Food tests are documented as experiments

externalPrerequisites.subject: Sachunterricht
externalPrerequisites.concept: healthy eating and food groups (Ernährungspyramide)
externalPrerequisites.reason: Kl. 5/6 adds nutrient chemistry and tests

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Digestion
topics.description: Pupils follow food through mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine, explain the division of labour between organs, model enzymes as 'scissors' that break nutrients into small building blocks, and explain the villi as surface enlargement for absorption into the blood.
evidence: Orders the digestive organs and states what happens in each
Explains with a simple model how enzymes break down starch
Explains why the folded small intestine absorbs nutrients efficiently
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} chewed a piece of bread for a long time and noticed it tasting sweet, could they explain what is happening and what happens to the bread afterwards?

prerequisites.reason: Digestion breaks down the nutrients learned before

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Breathing and Gas Exchange
topics.description: Pupils describe the airways and lungs, explain chest and abdominal breathing with a lung model (bell jar), and explain gas exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the alveoli as another case of surface enlargement.
evidence: Labels trachea, bronchi, lungs and alveoli
Explains inhalation using the diaphragm model
Describes the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between alveoli and blood
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} played with a bell-jar lung model, could they explain what the rubber sheet stands for and why the balloons fill with air?

prerequisites.reason: Breathing movements use rib and diaphragm muscles

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Heart, Blood and Circulation
topics.description: Pupils explain the heart as a double pump with atria, ventricles and valves, trace the body and lung circulation through arteries, capillaries and veins, describe blood components and their tasks, and measure pulse and breathing rate at rest and after exercise.
evidence: Traces the path of a red blood cell through lung and body circulation on a diagram
Names blood components and the task of each
Collects and graphs pulse data before and after exercise and explains the increase
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measured their pulse before and after running up the stairs, could they explain why it rises and what the blood is transporting faster?

prerequisites.reason: Lung circulation connects to gas exchange
Blood transports absorbed nutrients
Pulse experiment requires measuring and graphing

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Smoking and Addiction Prevention
topics.description: Pupils explain how nicotine, tar and carbon monoxide damage lungs, heart and blood vessels (including e-cigarettes), what addiction means, and develop strategies to say no under peer pressure; legal age limits come from the Jugendschutzgesetz.
evidence: Names three harmful substances in cigarette smoke and their effects
Explains what makes nicotine addictive
Role-plays or writes a convincing refusal strategy for a peer-pressure situation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If an older pupil offered {{name}} a vape at the bus stop, could they explain what it does to the body and how to say no without losing face?

prerequisites.reason: Damage is explained via lungs and gas exchange
Carbon monoxide and nicotine affect blood and vessels

osMatches.note: os 'Effects of Drugs & Alcohol' at age 13-14; Germany starts tobacco prevention at age 11-12

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Changes in Puberty
topics.description: Pupils describe physical changes in puberty (growth spurt, body hair, breasts, voice change, first period and first ejaculation) and emotional changes, understand that timing varies, and learn body care and hygiene.
evidence: Names physical changes in girls and boys during puberty
Describes emotional changes and that timing differs between individuals
Explains suitable hygiene measures for puberty
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s friend worried about being the only one in class whose voice had not changed yet, could they explain why puberty starts at different times?

externalPrerequisites.subject: Sachunterricht
externalPrerequisites.concept: primary sex education (body parts, growing up, where babies come from)
externalPrerequisites.reason: Sexualerziehung starts in Grundschule and is deepened in Kl. 5/6

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Sex Organs and the Menstrual Cycle
topics.description: Pupils name the male and female sex organs with correct terms and functions, explain egg and sperm cell production, describe the menstrual cycle (ovulation, menstruation) in outline, and reflect on respectful language about sexuality.

Describes the phases of the menstrual cycle and when ovulation happens
Uses correct terms instead of slang and explains why respectful language matters
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked by a younger sibling what a 'period' is, could they explain it correctly and respectfully in simple words?

prerequisites.reason: Organs and cycle explain the changes of puberty

osMatches.note: os 'Human Reproduction' at age 12-13 covers organs, cycle and pregnancy together

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Fertilisation, Pregnancy and Birth
topics.description: Pupils compare egg and sperm, describe fertilisation, the development of embryo and foetus, birth, risks to the unborn child (alcohol, smoking), and basic methods of contraception for responsible life planning.
evidence: Describes fertilisation and implantation in the right order
Describes key stages of embryo and foetus development and of birth
Explains why a pregnant woman should avoid alcohol and smoking, and names two contraceptive methods
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw ultrasound pictures from different months of a pregnancy, could they describe what is developing and why the mother avoids alcohol?

prerequisites.reason: Fertilisation requires knowing egg and sperm production

topics.laenderNotes: Contraception is explicit in NRW Kl. 5/6 (IF3) but not in BW BNT 5/6 (3.1.6), where it follows in later grades.

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Exploring a Local Habitat
topics.nameDe: Lebensraum erkunden: Hecke, Wald oder Wiese
topics.description: Pupils investigate a habitat near school (hedge, forest edge, meadow, pond), identify typical organisms with simple keys, collect and examine invertebrates gently, and record seasonal changes over the year in a field protocol.
evidence: Identifies at least five organisms of a local habitat with a key or app
Records observations at the same site in two seasons and compares them
Describes how the structure of the habitat (layers of a forest or hedge) offers niches to different animals
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} visited the hedge behind the school in autumn and in spring, could they record and explain what had changed for plants and animals?

prerequisites.reason: Identification keys are used in the field
Field observations are recorded in a protocol

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Food Chains, Webs and Decomposers
topics.description: Pupils build food chains and webs for a native habitat with producers, consumers and decomposers (earthworm, fungi, bacteria), and explain leaf-litter decomposition as nature's recycling that closes the cycle of materials.
evidence: Draws a food chain and a food web for a forest with correct arrow direction
Assigns organisms to producers, consumers and decomposers
Explains what happens to fallen leaves and why this matters for the forest
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wondered why the forest floor does not pile up metres high with leaves, could they explain who breaks them down and what happens to the nutrients?

prerequisites.reason: Food relations are studied in a known habitat
Producers make food from light

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Waste Separation and Recycling
topics.description: Pupils sort household waste into the German fractions (Wertstoff/Gelber Sack, paper, glass, organic, residual, hazardous waste such as batteries), separate a drinks carton into its layers, try a recycling process such as making paper, and evaluate their own waste avoidance.
evidence: Assigns typical household items to the correct bin and explains the material property behind it
Separates a composite drinks carton into paper, plastic and aluminium
Suggests two ways to avoid waste in their own daily life
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} had an empty yoghurt pot, a juice carton, a dead battery and apple peel, could they put each in the right bin and explain why?

prerequisites.reason: Sorting relies on material properties
Industrial sorting uses magnetic and density separation

topics.laenderNotes: Context is the German dual system (Gelber Sack/Wertstofftonne, deposit 'Pfand'); bin colours vary by municipality.

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Properties of Substances
topics.description: Pupils distinguish an object (Körper) from the substance (Stoff) it is made of and identify substances by properties such as colour, smell, hardness, deformability, solubility, electrical conductivity, magnetism and melting temperature, summarised in a Steckbrief.
evidence: Explains the difference between object and substance with examples
Tests at least four properties of an unknown substance and records them
Uses a property profile (Steckbrief) to identify a substance
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were given three white powders (sugar, salt, flour), could they plan tests based on properties to tell them apart?

prerequisites.reason: Properties are determined experimentally

externalPrerequisites.subject: Sachunterricht
externalPrerequisites.concept: materials and their properties (wood, metal, plastic, glass)
externalPrerequisites.reason: Kl. 5 moves from everyday materials to substance properties

osMatches.note: os object vs material at age 5-6

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Mass, Volume and Floating
topics.nameDe: Masse, Volumen und Dichte: Schwimmen, Schweben, Sinken
topics.description: Pupils measure mass with a balance and volume with a measuring cylinder or overflow method, and use a qualitative idea of density (heavy for its size) to explain why objects float, hover or sink in water.
evidence: Determines the volume of an irregular object by displacement
Explains why a large wooden block floats while a small iron nail sinks
Predicts and explains floating, hovering or sinking for given objects
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw a huge steel ship float but a steel coin sink, could they explain the difference using mass, volume and density?

prerequisites.reason: Requires measuring mass and volume
Density is a characteristic property of a substance

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: volume units (ml, l, cm³)
externalPrerequisites.reason: Volumes are read and converted

topics.laenderNotes: Floating/sinking is a BW BNT core topic (3.1.3); in NRW density appears in Physik later (Druck und Auftrieb).

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Mixtures and Solutions
topics.description: Pupils distinguish pure substances from mixtures (Gemenge, Lösung, Suspension, Emulsion), investigate water as a solvent (salt, sugar, mineral water) and recognise a saturated solution.
evidence: Classifies everyday products (orange juice, salad dressing, salt water, granite) as types of mixture
Shows experimentally that dissolved salt is still present
Explains what a saturated solution is
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} kept stirring salt into a glass of water until some stayed at the bottom, could they explain what happened and whether the salt has disappeared?

prerequisites.reason: Solubility is a substance property

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Separating Mixtures
topics.description: Pupils choose and carry out separation methods based on differing properties: sorting, sieving, magnetic separation, sedimenting and decanting, filtering, evaporating; and relate them to technical uses such as salt production or a sewage plant.
evidence: Separates a mixture of sand, salt and iron filings in a sensible order
Justifies each method by the property it exploits
Describes one technical application (water treatment or salt works)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were given a mixture of sand, salt and iron filings, could they plan and carry out steps to get all three back separately?

prerequisites.reason: One must know mixture types to choose a method
Evaporating requires heating

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: States of Matter and Changes of State
topics.description: Pupils name the three states and the six transitions (schmelzen, erstarren, verdampfen, kondensieren, sublimieren, resublimieren), record the heating curve of water and determine melting and boiling temperatures as substance properties.
evidence: Names all state transitions with the correct terms in a diagram
Records and interprets the temperature curve of heating water, including the boiling plateau
Uses melting and boiling points to predict the state of a substance at a given temperature
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heated ice until the water boiled while measuring the temperature, could they sketch the curve and explain why it stays flat at 0 °C and 100 °C?

prerequisites.reason: Melting and boiling points are measured with a thermometer

externalPrerequisites.subject: Sachunterricht
externalPrerequisites.concept: water as ice, liquid and steam; evaporation in the water cycle
externalPrerequisites.reason: Builds on primary knowledge of water states

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Simple Particle Model
topics.description: Pupils learn that substances consist of tiny moving particles and use this model to explain the three states, changes of state, dissolving and diffusion; they discuss where the model differs from reality (particles are not small balls of the substance).
evidence: Draws particle diagrams for solid, liquid and gas and explains the differences
Explains dissolving of sugar in tea with the particle model
Names one limitation of the particle model
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} noticed that a drop of ink spreads faster in hot water than in cold water, could they explain this with the particle model?

prerequisites.reason: The model explains the observed states and transitions
Dissolving is a key application

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Combustion and Fire Extinguishing
topics.description: Pupils investigate the conditions for burning (fuel, oxygen from the air, ignition temperature – the Verbrennungsdreieck) with candles and the burner, explain that combustion releases energy, and derive extinguishing methods by removing one condition.
evidence: Names the three conditions for combustion and shows each in a candle experiment
Explains why a candle under a glass goes out
Matches extinguishing methods (water, blanket, removing fuel) to the condition they remove
topics.assessmentPrompt: If oil in a pan caught fire, could {{name}} explain why a lid is the right choice and why water would be dangerous?

prerequisites.reason: Fire experiments require safety rules
Ignition experiments use the burner

osMatches.note: os combustion only as one reaction type at age 12-13

topics.laenderNotes: Combustion is BW BNT 3.1.4 (Kl. 5/6); NRW treats it in Chemie from Kl. 7.

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Measuring Temperature
topics.description: Pupils learn why the sense of warmth is unreliable, how a liquid thermometer works (thermal expansion), how the Celsius scale is defined by the fixed points 0 °C and 100 °C, and read analogue and digital thermometers correctly, including negative values.
evidence: Shows with three water bowls that the hand misjudges temperature
Reads analogue thermometers correctly at eye level, including below zero
Explains how the Celsius scale is defined
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} put one hand in cold and one in warm water and then both in lukewarm water, could they explain the strange feeling and why we use thermometers?

prerequisites.reason: Temperature measurement applies general measuring rules

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: reading scales and number lines, including values below zero
externalPrerequisites.reason: Thermometer reading uses scale reading

osMatches.note: os age 5-7, without the definition of the scale

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Temperature versus Heat
topics.description: Pupils distinguish temperature (how hot a body is, measured in °C) from heat (energy transferred from a hotter to a colder body) and describe temperature equalisation until thermal equilibrium, using everyday technical language precisely.
evidence: Uses 'temperature' and 'heat' correctly in explanations
Predicts the final temperature trend when hot and cold water are mixed
Explains why a metal spoon in hot tea gets warm
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} left a cup of hot cocoa on the table, could they explain where the heat goes and when the cooling stops?

prerequisites.reason: Temperature must be understood as a measurable quantity first

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Thermal Expansion
topics.description: Pupils observe that solids, liquids and gases expand when heated, explain this with the particle model, give technical examples (expansion joints on bridges, bimetal strip) and describe the anomaly of water (densest at 4 °C) and why lakes freeze from the top.
evidence: Explains thermal expansion with the particle model
Gives two technical examples where expansion must be considered
Explains why fish survive the winter at the bottom of a frozen lake
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw gaps between sections of a railway bridge, could they explain why engineers build them and what would happen without them?

prerequisites.reason: Expansion is explained by particle motion
The thermometer is an application of expansion

osMatches.note: os bundles thermal expansion with deformation and fluid pressure at age 12-13

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Heat Transfer and Insulation
topics.description: Pupils distinguish the three ways heat travels – Wärmeleitung (conduction), Wärmemitführung (convection) and Wärmestrahlung (radiation) – and explain insulation in houses, thermos flasks, clothing and animal fur or feathers.
evidence: Assigns everyday situations (radiator, sunbathing, hot pan handle) to the correct type of heat transfer
Tests materials for insulation in a fair comparison
Explains how a thermos flask or a bird's plumage reduces heat loss
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compared a woolly hat and a thin cap on a cold day, could they explain which type of heat transfer the hat reduces and why trapped air helps?

prerequisites.reason: Heat transfer presupposes the concept of heat
Insulation tests require fair comparison

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Energy Forms and Conversion Chains
topics.description: Pupils describe energy chains in nature (Sun → plant → human) and technology (power station → household), distinguish fossil and renewable energy carriers, understand that energy is converted rather than used up, and derive energy-saving rules such as Stoßlüften and switching off devices.
evidence: Draws an energy conversion chain for a given device or food chain
Classifies energy carriers as fossil or renewable
Derives and justifies three energy-saving rules for school or home
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} ate a bowl of muesli and then cycled to school, could they trace the energy back to the Sun in a chain of conversions?

prerequisites.reason: Heat is the first energy form studied
Plants store solar energy
Electrical devices convert energy

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Closed Circuits, Conductors and Insulators
topics.nameDe: Der elektrische Stromkreis: Leiter und Nichtleiter
topics.description: Pupils build closed circuits with a source, consumers and switches, test which materials conduct, and explain current with a simple model of freely moving electrons in metals.
evidence: Builds a working circuit with battery, lamp and switch and explains why it must be closed
Tests materials and classifies them as conductors or insulators
Explains with the electron model why current flows only in a closed loop
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} had a battery, a bulb, wires and a set of objects, could they find out which objects let current through and explain the result?

prerequisites.reason: Conductivity is a substance property

externalPrerequisites.subject: Sachunterricht
externalPrerequisites.concept: simple circuit with battery, wires and bulb
externalPrerequisites.reason: Primary school introduces the closed circuit

topics.laenderNotes: NRW Physik and BB Naturwissenschaften 5/6 (Themenfeld 3.9 Technik) treat circuits in Kl. 5/6; BW BNT 5/6 has no circuit standard, electricity follows in Physik from Kl. 7.

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Circuit Symbols and Diagrams
topics.description: Pupils use the standard circuit symbols (cell/battery, lamp, switch, motor, buzzer, wire) to draw circuit diagrams with straight lines and build circuits from given diagrams.
evidence: Draws a correct circuit diagram for a built circuit using standard symbols
Builds a circuit from a given diagram
Finds the fault in a diagram that cannot work
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were given a circuit diagram with a battery, two lamps and a switch, could they build it and say what happens when the switch is opened?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Series and Parallel Circuits

evidence: Predicts and tests what happens in series and parallel circuits when one lamp is unscrewed
Explains why devices at home are wired in parallel
Designs an AND or an OR circuit for a given task
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked to wire a bell that rings when either the front or the back door button is pressed, could they draw and build the right circuit?

prerequisites.reason: Branched circuits are planned with diagrams

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Effects of Current and Electrical Safety

topics.description: Pupils describe the heating, lighting and magnetic effects of current with device examples, explain short circuits and how fuses and circuit breakers protect, and know why mains electricity (230 V) and overhead railway lines are life-threatening.
evidence: Names a device for each effect of electric current
Explains what a short circuit is and how a fuse protects the circuit
States rules for safe use of electrical devices and checks a device for visible damage

topics.name: Magnets and Magnetic Materials

evidence: Predicts attraction or repulsion between given poles
Sorts materials into magnetic and non-magnetic
Explains magnetising a nail and breaking a magnet in two with the Elementarmagnet model
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} broke a bar magnet in half, could they predict whether they get a separate north and south pole and explain why with a model?

externalPrerequisites.subject: Sachunterricht
externalPrerequisites.concept: magnets attract objects made of iron

topics.name: Magnetic Fields and the Compass
topics.description: Pupils make magnetic fields visible with iron filings and small compasses, draw field-line patterns, and explain the compass needle as a small magnet aligning with Earth's magnetic field.
evidence: Draws the field-line pattern of a bar magnet from an iron-filings experiment
Explains why a compass needle points north
Builds a simple compass from a magnetised needle

Compass use in Erdkunde links to its physical explanation

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: How Light Travels and How We See

Explains with a ray diagram why we see a book in a lit room but not in total darkness
Explains why a pinhole camera image is upside down

Explains core and half shadow with two lamps
Explains why shadows have the shape of the object

Justifies why a reflector makes a cyclist visible to drivers

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften

Gives examples of ultrasound in nature and medicine

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften

evidence: Explains why there is no sound in a vacuum

Proposes and justifies noise-protection measures for a classroom or street
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measured the noise in the school canteen with a phone app, could they judge whether it is harmful and suggest ways to make it quieter?

Propagation is explained with particles

topics.subject: Erdkunde
